title: How We Knew Light Bends — Eddington's 1919 Eclipse Expedition
topic: general relativity / 1919 solar eclipse / Eddington / Dyson / Sobral / Príncipe
tone: engaged scientific explainer (Veritasium without the host); third-person declarative, second-person rare; document-led
hook: On the morning of May 29, 1919, on a volcanic island off the coast of West Africa, an English astronomer named Arthur Eddington pointed a four-inch telescope at a total solar eclipse — and proved Albert Einstein right.
narration:
On the morning of May 29, 1919, on a volcanic island off the coast of West Africa, an English astronomer named Arthur Eddington pointed a four-inch telescope at a total solar eclipse — and proved Albert Einstein right.

This is the story of how the most famous theory in physics came to be tested. It is a story about photographs. About a piece of glass laid against another piece of glass on a measuring engine in Cambridge. About a measurement so small you could not see it with the naked eye, and so consequential that within a week of its announcement, the New York Times put the words 'Lights All Askew in the Heavens' on its front page.

It is also a story about how a single number — one point seven five — overturned more than two centuries of Newtonian physics, and made an obscure German-Swiss patent clerk into the most famous scientist who has ever lived.

This is how we knew light bends.

--- CHAPTER 1: PREDICTION ---

In nineteen-fifteen, Albert Einstein was not yet Einstein. He was a thirty-six-year-old physicist working in Berlin, on the wartime staff of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute. He had spent the previous eight years trying to extend his nineteen-oh-five theory of special relativity into something that could describe gravity. And in November of nineteen-fifteen, after a sequence of four lectures delivered to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, he had it. The general theory of relativity.

The central equation Einstein wrote down — published in full in his nineteen-sixteen paper in Annalen der Physik, titled 'Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie' — said something extraordinary. Mass does not pull on objects through some invisible force at a distance, the way Newton had described two and a half centuries earlier. Mass curves the geometry of spacetime itself. And anything moving through that curved geometry — including a beam of light — must follow the curves.

This was not a small claim. Newton's theory of gravitation had been the most successful idea in the history of physics. It had predicted the return of Halley's Comet. It had explained the motion of every planet in the solar system. It had let engineers calculate the trajectory of an artillery shell and the orbit of the Moon. To say that Newton was incomplete — that gravity was not a force at all but a property of geometry — was to ask the entire scientific establishment to reconsider its foundations.

Einstein knew this. And so he proposed three specific, falsifiable tests.

The first was already passing. Mercury's orbit precesses around the Sun by a tiny amount each century — about forty-three arcseconds beyond what Newton predicted. Astronomers had been puzzling over this anomaly since the eighteen-fifties. When Einstein plugged Mercury's orbit into his new field equations, the unexplained forty-three arcseconds fell out exactly. He wrote later that the discovery gave him heart palpitations.

The second test was gravitational redshift — the prediction that light climbing out of a gravitational well loses energy and shifts toward longer wavelengths. This would not be confirmed in a laboratory until the nineteen-fifty-nine Pound-Rebka experiment in a tower at Harvard, forty years later.

But the third test was the one anyone could see. If mass curves spacetime, then a star whose light grazes the limb of the Sun on its way to Earth should appear to be in slightly the wrong place. The light from that star should bend.

Einstein had calculated this deflection twice. His first attempt, in nineteen-eleven, had used only the equivalence principle — the idea that gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable. It produced a value of zero point eight seven arcseconds. That was the same value Newton's theory would predict if you treated light as a stream of particles falling under gravity.

But by nineteen-fifteen, with the full field equations, Einstein realised he had missed something. Spacetime is curved in space as well as in time. The full deflection had to account for both. He recalculated. The answer doubled.

One point seven five arcseconds. Twice the Newtonian value.

This is the document — page eight hundred and four of Annalen der Physik, volume three hundred and fifty-four, issue seven, published nineteen-sixteen — where the prediction lives. And this is the number that anyone watching a total solar eclipse, with a precise enough telescope, could in principle measure. During totality, the Moon blocks the disc of the Sun completely. For a few minutes, stars near the Sun's limb become visible. If you photograph them during the eclipse, then photograph the same patch of sky months later when the Sun is somewhere else, and lay the two plates against each other, the stars in the eclipse plate will be displaced — pushed outward, away from where the Sun was. By how much? If Newton is right, by zero point eight seven arcseconds. If Einstein is right, by one point seven five.

A factor of two.

There was, in fact, almost an attempt. In August of nineteen-fourteen, a German astronomer named Erwin Freundlich travelled to the Crimea, in the south of the Russian Empire, to photograph a total solar eclipse and test exactly the deflection Einstein had calculated. Freundlich's instruments were paid for by, of all people, the founder of the Krupp armaments firm — Gustav Krupp had given Einstein a private grant of two thousand marks specifically to fund the test. The expedition reached Crimea. It set up its telescope. It waited for August twenty-first.

On July twenty-eighth, three weeks before totality, the First World War began. Freundlich, a German national in Russian territory, was arrested as an enemy alien. His instruments were confiscated. He was eventually exchanged in a prisoner swap and sent home. The eclipse, when it came, was photographed by no one capable of measuring star positions on its plates.

This was, in retrospect, a kind of luck for Einstein. The nineteen-fourteen calculation he had handed Freundlich was based on his earlier, incomplete theory — the one giving zero point eight seven arcseconds. If Freundlich had measured anything close to the correct value, Einstein's prediction at the time would have been refuted. By the time he completed the field equations in nineteen-fifteen and corrected the prediction to one point seven five, no one had been able to test either number.

It would be five more years before anyone tried again. And the people who tried — at the highest levels of the British scientific establishment — would belong to the country that had spent four years at war with Einstein's.

--- CHAPTER 2: EXPERIMENT ---

In March of nineteen-nineteen, four months after the armistice, two ships left England.

One sailed south to Brazil. The other to a small Portuguese island in the Gulf of Guinea. Their mission was identical. On May twenty-ninth, the Moon's shadow would sweep a narrow path across the equatorial Atlantic, and for almost seven minutes — an unusually long totality, one of the longest the twentieth century would offer — the Sun would be perfectly eclipsed. The eclipsed disc would lie squarely against a bright cluster of stars: the Hyades, in the constellation Taurus. Bright. Numerous. Photographable.

It was the best opportunity to test general relativity that anyone alive would see for decades.

It is worth pausing on the political shape of this. The British Empire had spent more than four years fighting the German Empire. Eight hundred and eighty thousand British soldiers had died on the Western Front. Einstein was a German-Swiss physicist who had renounced his German citizenship at sixteen, then taken Prussian citizenship in nineteen-fourteen to accept his post in Berlin. His theory had been published, in German, by a German journal, during the war. And here was the senior staff of the Royal Greenwich Observatory, six months after the armistice, organising an expedition to test that theory at British public expense.

This was not lost on contemporary commentators. Several British newspapers, in the spring of nineteen-nineteen, ran editorials questioning whether the Astronomer Royal should be diverting resources to verify the work of an enemy national. Dyson, who had spent the war calculating precise time signals for Royal Navy navigation, was unmoved. Eddington, whose Quakerism had already made him a controversial figure for refusing combat service, framed the expedition as a kind of restoration — that proving an enemy scientist right would, in his words, repair some of the damage that the war had done to the international fellowship of science.

The expedition had been organised by Sir Frank Watson Dyson — Astronomer Royal, director of the Royal Greenwich Observatory, and the man whose photograph you are looking at now. Dyson had recognised three years earlier, in nineteen-seventeen, with the war still on, that the nineteen-nineteen eclipse offered an exceptional star field and exceptional duration. He had funded the planning. He had selected the two stations. He had assigned the personnel.

The Brazilian station, at Sobral, in the state of Ceará, was led by Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson, both senior staff at Greenwich. They carried two telescopes. The primary instrument was a four-inch astrographic refractor — the same type of telescope that had been used to map the southern sky for the international Carte du Ciel project. The secondary was a separate four-inch lens by the optician Father Aloysius Cortie, mounted on its own telescope.

The Príncipe station was led by Arthur Eddington himself, accompanied by the engineer Edwin Cottingham. Eddington was thirty-six years old, the Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge, and — crucially — he was a Quaker. During the war he had refused conscription on religious grounds. He had spent nineteen-eighteen working out, in the pages of the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the implications of Einstein's new field equations. He was, by some measure, the only man in the British Empire who fully understood what the expedition was trying to test.

The Príncipe team set up at the Roça Sundy plantation, a cocoa estate on the northern shore of the island. The Sobral team took rooms on the central square of the small market town. By mid-May, both telescopes were aligned, both photographic plates were in their holders, both teams were rehearsing the exposure sequence.

May twenty-ninth arrived.

At Príncipe, the morning was clouded over. The previous night a tropical thunderstorm had passed across the island; by dawn the rain had stopped but the cloud cover had not lifted. Eddington wrote in his diary: 'There was nothing for it but to carry out the prearranged programme and hope for the best.' Totality began at one-fifty-five in the afternoon, local time. The team exposed sixteen plates in succession across the next three hundred and two seconds. Most of them — Eddington would later count — captured nothing but cloud. Only two plates showed star images, and even on those two, only a handful of the brightest Hyades stars were visible. Two plates, out of sixteen, with five stars between them. That was the entire Príncipe yield.

In his diary that evening, Eddington wrote a single short sentence that historians have since spent a great deal of ink interpreting: 'The cloud has interfered very much with the star images. The first plate I measured gave a result agreeing with Einstein.' He does not say whether this was a relief or a confirmation. He does not say whether it changed his confidence in the prediction. He simply records the number.

At Sobral, the weather was clear. The astrographic refractor — the primary instrument — exposed nineteen plates during totality. But something had gone wrong with the telescope's mirror. The Brazilian heat, combined with hours of bright sunlight before the eclipse, had distorted the figure of the coelostat mirror that fed light into the telescope. When Crommelin developed the plates, the star images were soft and out of focus. Useless for precision measurement.

The campaign was now resting on the Sobral Cortie lens.

That lens — the smaller, secondary instrument, treated almost as a backup — was mounted independently of the failed coelostat. Its plates came out sharp. Seven plates, with crisp star images, captured during totality on May twenty-ninth.

But here is something the popular telling of this story usually leaves out. You will sometimes hear that Eddington's Príncipe plates were the ones that confirmed relativity. That is not quite true. The Príncipe plates were the ones Eddington reduced first, in early June, on the island, on a portable measuring device. He did get a result — about one and a half arcseconds, with substantial error bars. He cabled the news to Dyson. He went home.

The sharper measurement came later. From Sobral. From the Cortie lens.

The Sobral plates were shipped to Greenwich. They arrived in late July. Through the late summer and autumn of nineteen-nineteen, Davidson and Eddington worked at the Royal Observatory and at Cambridge on a Zeiss measuring engine — a precision optical instrument with a cross-haired eyepiece, micrometer screws calibrated to the micron, and a brass plate stage onto which two photographic plates could be clamped face to face. The plates from totality were laid against comparison plates of the same Hyades star field, taken in January and February of nineteen-nineteen at Greenwich and at Oxford, when the Sun was on the other side of the sky and the Hyades were visible in the night.

Each star's position on the eclipse plate was compared to its position on the comparison plate. The differences were measured to within hundredths of an arcsecond. The plates were also rotated through a hundred and eighty degrees and remeasured, to cancel out any systematic errors in the measuring engine itself. Each star generated four numbers. The numbers were tabulated, by hand, in ledger sheets that survive in the Royal Astronomical Society archives in London.

This is the moment of measurement. Two pieces of glass, face to face, in a brass-and-iron measuring frame, lit from below by an oil lamp. A man with a magnifying eyepiece, tabulating the small displacement of fifteen stars across two plates, by hand, in a ledger. There is no electronic detector. There is no computer. There is no automated plate scanner. There is the eye of one trained astronomer, the position of one star, and the slow accumulation of a number.

The Sobral Cortie lens result: one point nine eight arcseconds, with an uncertainty of zero point one two.

The Príncipe Eddington result, despite its small sample: one point six one arcseconds, with an uncertainty of zero point three zero.

The Newtonian prediction, zero point eight seven, was excluded by the Sobral measurement at more than nine standard deviations.

The Einsteinian prediction, one point seven five, sat comfortably within the error bars of both.

There was — and this is the chapter's mythbust — a third set of plates, from the Sobral astrographic refractor, the failed primary instrument. Those plates, when reduced anyway, gave a value of zero point nine three arcseconds — close to the Newtonian prediction, far from Einstein. Some historians have argued that Eddington and Dyson's decision to discard the astrographic plates as unreliable was a closer call than the published paper suggests, and that Eddington's prior commitment to general relativity may have influenced the cut. The standard rebuttal, made carefully by historians like Daniel Kennefick in his two thousand and nineteen book, is that the astrographic mirror's distortion was independently documented, that the plates really were soft, and that excluding them was the correct call regardless of which theory was being tested. The criticism is real, but the conclusion holds: the Sobral Cortie data, on its own, settles the question.

On November sixth, nineteen-nineteen, at Burlington House in London, the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society held a joint meeting. The chair was J. J. Thomson — the man who had discovered the electron twenty-two years earlier, and the President of the Royal Society. Dyson rose first, presented the data, walked the audience through the plate measurements, and concluded that the results confirmed Einstein's prediction.

Thomson stood. He looked at the audience. And he said: 'This is the most important result obtained in connection with the theory of gravitation since Newton's day.'

The room was silent for a moment. Then it erupted.

--- CHAPTER 3: CONSEQUENCE ---

The news travelled fast.

The Times of London ran the story the next morning, November seventh. The headline — set in serif type three columns wide — read: 'Revolution in Science. New Theory of the Universe. Newtonian Ideas Overthrown.'

Three days later, the New York Times did the same. Their headline, on page seventeen of the November tenth edition, was even more breathless: 'Lights All Askew in the Heavens. Men of Science More or Less Agog Over Results of Eclipse Observations.' A subheadline added, almost apologetically, 'Einstein Theory Triumphs.'

Until that week, Einstein had been a mostly continental celebrity, known primarily within physics journals. By November fourteenth, he was a global household name. Photographers waited outside his Berlin apartment. Reporters cabled questions in from London, Paris, New York. He had not become a different physicist. The world had become a different audience.

The physics of the eclipse, it turned out, had been the easy part. The much longer story — the story the rest of the twentieth century would tell — was about reconfirming what those plates had shown. In nineteen-fifty-nine, two physicists at Harvard, Robert Pound and Glen Rebka, used the recently discovered Mössbauer effect — a phenomenon in which iron-fifty-seven nuclei, embedded in a crystal lattice, emit gamma rays at an extraordinarily precise frequency — to measure the gravitational redshift of gamma rays falling down a twenty-two-metre tower in the Jefferson Physical Laboratory. The frequency shift they were trying to detect was about two parts in ten to the fifteenth. They detected it. Einstein's prediction held to within ten percent. Three years later, an improved version of the experiment closed the agreement to within one percent. In nineteen-seventy-one, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating put atomic clocks on commercial airliners and flew them around the world in opposite directions. The clocks, when they returned, disagreed with the clocks they had left behind by exactly the amount general relativity said they should. In two thousand and three, the Cassini spacecraft, on its way to Saturn, transmitted radio signals that grazed the Sun's gravitational field — and the Doppler shift in those signals confirmed Einstein's prediction to a precision of two parts in one hundred thousand. By the time of Gravity Probe B in twenty-eleven, which used four spinning gyroscopes orbiting the Earth in a polar drag-free satellite to measure the way the rotation of our planet drags spacetime around with it, every prediction Einstein made in the nineteen-sixteen paper had been verified, repeatedly, to extraordinary precision. And in twenty-fifteen, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory in Hanford, Washington and Livingston, Louisiana, detected the merger of two black holes a billion light-years away, recording a strain pattern that matched a numerical solution of Einstein's field equations almost shape for shape — a confirmation a hundred years to the month after the field equations had been completed.

And in nineteen-eighty-nine, with the deployment of the Global Positioning System, the engineering profession finally had to start using general relativity for real work. GPS satellites orbit at twenty thousand kilometres altitude, in a weaker gravitational field than the surface of the Earth. Their atomic clocks, sitting in that weaker field, run faster than clocks on the ground by about forty-five microseconds per day from the gravitational effect, and slower by about seven microseconds per day from the velocity-related time dilation predicted by special relativity. Net difference: thirty-eight microseconds per day. If GPS receivers did not correct for that — and the correction was built into the system from the start, on the basis of Einstein's nineteen-sixteen field equations — your position fix would drift by about eleven kilometres per day.

Thirty-eight microseconds. That is the engineering legacy of the man with the magnifying eyepiece in Cambridge, ninety years earlier, measuring the displacement of a Hyades star on a piece of glass. Every time a phone navigates, every time an aircraft transponds its position, every time a delivery truck calculates an arrival window, the equations Eddington tested are doing real work.

In two thousand and three, the Cassini spacecraft, on its way to Saturn, passed behind the Sun from Earth's perspective. Engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory tracked the shift in the timing of Cassini's radio signals as those signals grazed the Sun's gravitational field. The result, published in Nature later that year by Bertotti, Iess and Tortora, agreed with general relativity to a precision of two parts in one hundred thousand. That paper is the strongest single confirmation of the deflection effect Eddington measured. The Cassini value, expressed in the language of the post-Newtonian formalism that physicists now use to test theories of gravity, gives a coefficient of one plus gamma equal to two point zero zero zero zero two one, plus or minus zero point zero zero zero zero two three. Two point zero zero zero zero two one. Five-decimal agreement with Einstein, eighty-four years after a cloudy morning on Príncipe.

There is one more part of this story worth telling. On November ninth, nineteen-twenty-two, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the nineteen-twenty-one Nobel Prize in Physics to Albert Einstein. It had been held over from the previous year because the committee could not agree. The official citation reads: 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' Relativity is conspicuously absent. The committee considered the eclipse evidence, even three years on, to be insufficient for a claim so radical, and chose the safer, narrower work on the photoelectric effect instead. Einstein, who was on a lecture tour in Japan when the announcement came, accepted the prize and donated the money to his estranged first wife, Mileva, as part of their nineteen-nineteen divorce settlement. He never delivered the conventional Nobel address on the photoelectric effect. He delivered one — in Gothenburg, in nineteen-twenty-three — on general relativity.

If you have made it this far, the channel runs on the kind of patient curiosity you have just demonstrated. Hitting like sends a small signal to YouTube that this kind of long-form physics is worth showing to other people. It costs nothing and it helps the work continue.

And that, more than anything, is how we knew. Not from a single dramatic moment of revelation. But from a handful of seven-minute exposures, on glass plates carried home in a steamer trunk from a Brazilian market town, measured by hand at a Cambridge bench, against a comparison plate of the same patch of sky taken six months earlier. From a number — one point nine eight, plus or minus zero point one two — that excluded one centuries-old theory and confirmed another.

One point nine eight arcseconds.

The smallest measurement that has ever changed the world.
